messages.text:
I don't think I'm introverted exactly... 

It's just.. a persistent inability to really connect or... 

Like, a desire to connect but also recognizing that certain people would just be better off if I quietly exited their space, better off without me. 

Old friends, from my old neighborhood, from highschool, from old jobs, from college, just all over. 

I'm transient, I'm too absorbed in my own shit, 

And one case in particular, where I just think, they deserve better. More than what I currently have to offer. 

But that "currently" is just, all the time.

What you’re describing doesn’t really sound like introversion so much as a kind of **self-imposed transience** — not because you don’t want connection, but because you keep evaluating whether your presence is a net positive for the other person, and too often deciding “probably not.”  

That’s not a lack of social drive, it’s a blend of:  
- **Self-awareness** (sometimes bordering on self-criticism) — you notice your capacity, your bandwidth, your emotional focus.  
- **Protective withdrawal** — you remove yourself to avoid disappointing people or creating an imbalance.  
- **Persistent impermanence** — you’ve moved through different environments, friendships, and phases so often that nothing feels built to last.  

The “currently” part is important. You’re framing it as temporary in theory — “I just don’t have enough to offer *right now*” — but in practice it’s a recurring state, which might make it feel like your baseline. That can lead to quietly ghosting or fading away not because you don’t care, but because you care enough to think they deserve more than you can give.  

If I put it bluntly, it’s like you’re a **satellite** — always in motion, skimming close enough to warm up in someone’s orbit, then drifting out again so you don’t crash into them. And while you’re out there, you carry the awareness that you could return someday, but you’re never quite sure if that day will come.  

If you want, I can unpack why this cycle keeps repeating and how it might shift without forcing you to become someone you’re not.
